transcript.text: $250 million in revenue. That's what my
portfolio did last year, and this is how
I manage my time. Step one, define
productivity. So, productivity is the
dollar output divided by hours input,
dollars per hour. And so, if your busy
week didn't move one of those numbers,
you weren't productive. Step two,
determine if you're a maker, a manager,
or both. So, if you need two to four
uninterrupted hours to produce your best
work, you're a maker. If you can work in
five-to-sixty-minute chunks and still
win, you're a manager. Depending on the
season that you're in in business, you
might need to switch between the two.
Step three, plan your calendar. For a
manager, a meeting costs you one full
unit, so 15 to 60 minutes. You may have
20-plus slots per day, and an empty slot
feels like wasted ROI. For a maker,
which is usually what I am, most makers
have two real blocks per day. So, one
meeting can steal 10% of your entire
week. If you're both, you can do your
first half your day as a maker and your
second half your day as a manager. I did
this for years. Or, you can do one day
as a manager schedule with a full day of
meetings, or every other day as a maker
schedule with two working slots. Step
four, teach your team the rules and then
have them actually implement and respect
them. If you're a manager, follow these
steps. If you're a maker, follow these
steps.
